rows.speaker: JJ
rows.claim: An omitted comparison completes the opening: is the expanded person like one without faith, or like one whose heart is sealed?
rows.anchor: “[is he] like he who is not” or “[is he] like one whose heart He has sealed” (JJ)

rows.speaker: Bḍ
rows.claim: The breast is the locus of the heart and fountainhead of the spirit, and so the seat of inspirations, thoughts, and intentions.
rows.anchor: the locus of the heart and the fountainhead of the spirit (Bḍ)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran connects the breast with what God knows within people and with the disclosure of inner contents on Judgment Day.
rows.anchor: The Quran mentions frequently that God knows what lies within breasts

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Breast expansion is associated with belief, while contraction is associated with disbelief.
rows.anchor: While the breast’s expansion is associated with belief

rows.speaker: Bḍ
rows.claim: Following light from God means that God has opened the heart to spiritual knowledge, or maʿrifah, and guidance.
rows.anchor: God has opened one’s heart to spiritual knowledge(maʿrifah ) and guidance (Bḍ)

rows.speaker: The Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet says light entering the heart makes it spacious; its sign is turning toward the eternal abode, shunning delusion, and preparing for death.
rows.anchor: The Prophet: “When light enters the heart, it expands and it becomes spacious.”

words: فَوَيْلٌۭ لِّلْقَٰسِيَةِ قُلُوبُهُم مِّن ذِكْرِ ٱللَّهِ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hardened hearts remain in dark desire and pursue worldly things, far from the lights of knowledge and guidance.
rows.anchor: stew in the dark recesses of desire and seek the things of this world

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hearts become hardened, sealed, or covered through wrongdoing and loss of Divine Favor, making them unreceptive to revelation and remembrance; Moses even asks that Pharaoh’s people be hardened.
rows.anchor: “hardened,” “sealed,” or “covered” as a result of their own wrongdoing and the consequent loss of Divine Favor

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The most beautiful discourse is the Quran, beautiful in both meaning and expression; its consimilar and paired verses display that beauty.
rows.anchor: The most beautiful discourse refers to the Quran (Bḍ, IK, Q), which is considered most beautiful in both meaning and expression

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: One reading of consimilar is that each part of the Quran is as eloquent as every other part.
rows.anchor: each part is as eloquent as the next (R)

rows.speaker: IK, Ṭ
rows.claim: Another reading is that many Quranic parts resemble one another through recurring phrases.
rows.anchor: with various recurring phrases (IK, Ṭ)

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Consimilarity may mean that qualities such as beauty and wisdom recur throughout the Quran.
rows.anchor: particular qualities such as beauty and wisdom (Q)

rows.speaker: Bḍ
rows.claim: Consimilarity may mean that truth and inimitability are found throughout the Quran.
rows.anchor: truth and inimitability (Bḍ) are found throughout

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: A further explanation is that each part confirms the other parts.
rows.anchor: each part confirms the other parts (Q)

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: Mutashābih also describes some Quranic verses in 3:7, where it carries a distinct technical meaning.
rows.anchor: used to describe some verses of the Quran in 3:7, but with a very different, more technical meaning of the word (IK)

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: Paired refers to Quranic juxtapositions of opposites, such as Heaven and Hell, believers and disbelievers, and reward and punishment.
rows.anchor: many opposites are juxtaposed in the Quran, such as Heaven and Hell

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The paired contrast is illustrated by skin quivering in fear of divine might and punishment, then skin and hearts softening in hope of mercy and forgiveness.
rows.anchor: skin that quivers out of fear of God’s Might and Punishment and the skins and hearts that soften

rows.speaker: Aj
rows.claim: The Quran’s power to make skins quiver and then soften with hearts is another attribute of its beauty.
rows.anchor: That the Quran makes skins quiver and then soften along with hearts is another attribute that makes it most beautiful (Aj)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other verses mention hearts responding to Quran recitation or God’s mention, but this is the only verse that describes skins quivering and softening.
rows.anchor: this is the only verse to mention those whose skins quiver and soften unto the remembrance of God

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Some commentators identify the people described as the Prophet’s Companions, whose eyes watered and skins quivered when the Quran was recited.
rows.anchor: According to some commentators, this is a description of the Companions of the Prophet

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: In the Companions interpretation, remembrance can mean the Quran as Reminder, one of its names being al-Dhikr.
rows.anchor: remembrance is often understood to mean “Reminder,” as a reference to the Quran

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The translation takes remembrance as remembrance of God, as in the verse describing believing hearts at peace in God’s remembrance.
rows.anchor: as translated here, it is understood as a reference to the remembrance of God referred to in such verses as 13:28

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another possible sense is that when God remembers a person, that person’s heart necessarily softens.
rows.anchor: when God remembers a person, that person’s heart cannot but soften

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: That is God’s Guidance can refer to the Quran described in the verse.
rows.anchor: That is God’s Guidance refers to the Quran as described in this verse (Q)

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Alternatively, it can refer to the fear of God’s punishment and hope for His reward that He grants.
rows.anchor: what God has granted by way of fear of His Punishment and hope for His Reward (Q)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran repeatedly says the astray have no way, guide, or protector; here this means one whose skin and heart do not soften has no guidance.

rows.speaker: IK, Ṭ
rows.claim: An omitted comparison asks whether this person is like one who does right; parallel contrasts appear in 41:40 and 67:22.
rows.anchor: in security on the Day of Resurrection? (IK, Ṭ) and 67:22

rows.speaker: Q, Ṭ
rows.claim: Guarding with his face may mean that the face is the first part to touch the Fire.
rows.anchor: the first thing to touch the Fire is his face or that he is dragged upon his face into the Fire (Q, Ṭ)

rows.speaker: Q, Ṭ
rows.claim: Alternatively, the phrase may describe someone dragged into the Fire on his face.
rows.anchor: he is dragged upon his face into the Fire (Q, Ṭ)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Taste that which you used to earn echoes the punishment statement in 7:39.
rows.anchor: evokes a similar statement in 7:39:

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: The opening asks whether God sufficed Muhammad as He had sufficed the prophets before him.
rows.anchor: Did not God suffice Muhammad, as He sufficed the prophets before him?

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: The idolaters thought that invoking their idols’ displeasure and wrath could influence the Prophet.
rows.anchor: their idols’ displeasure and wrath will somehow influence the Prophet (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: His servant can mean any believer: God suffices those who worship only Him and rely solely upon Him.
rows.anchor: can also be understood to mean any believer, meaning that God suffices for anyone who worships only Him and relies solely upon Him (IK)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The assurance follows the analogy in 39:29: monotheism frees the believer from divided masters and scattered aspirations, since God provides all that is needed.
rows.anchor: In this sense, it follows upon the analogy of v. 29

words: وَمَن يُضْلِلِ ٱللَّهُ فَمَا لَهُۥ مِنْ هَادٍ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who do not believe and trust God are left astray, without a way, guide, or protector, and are losers.
rows.anchor: The one who does not believe and trust in God is allowed to go astray and has no way

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Whomever God guides is rightly guided, and none can undo that guidance because God is powerful over all things.
rows.anchor: whomsoever God guides, he is rightly guided (7:178; 17:97; 18:17)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s might and vengeance mean that, unlike the idols invoked against the Prophet, God will punish those who deny Him.
rows.anchor: God will have vengeance upon those who deny Him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pattern of calling on God in hardship and turning away when relieved is repeated elsewhere in the Quran.

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Turning to God in need, then growing arrogant with blessing, exposes corruption: people acknowledge God alone protects them, then credit their gains to their own striving.
rows.anchor: they have in effect acknowledged that none but God can protect them from what afflicts them

rows.speaker: IK, R
rows.claim: One interpretation is that God gave the blessings because He knew the recipient deserved them.
rows.anchor: “I was given these blessings because God knew that I deserved them” (IK, R)

rows.speaker: IK, Q
rows.claim: Another interpretation is that the recipient claims to have received blessings because of a special position.
rows.anchor: “because I have a special position” (IK, Q)

rows.speaker: IK, R
rows.claim: The claim may mean that the recipient himself knew that he deserved the blessings.
rows.anchor: “because I myself knew that I deserved them”(IK, R)

rows.speaker: Q, R
rows.claim: Alternatively, the speaker says his own knowledge earned him the benefit.
rows.anchor: “because my own knowledge earned this benefit for me” (Q, R)

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: A further interpretation is that the blessing came because of knowledge God had taught the recipient.
rows.anchor: “because of some knowledge that God has taught me” (Q)

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Blessings are a trial requiring gratitude while they last and patience when they disappear.
rows.anchor: Such blessings are a trial from God because one must manifest gratitude upon receiving them and patience upon their disappearance (R)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The earlier people repeated the claim from 39:49 that they received blessings because of knowledge, like Korah in 28:78.
rows.anchor: The same refers to the statement I was only given it because of knowledge in v. 49

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Korah, described as a wealthy member of Pharaoh’s court, makes a similar claim in 28:78.
rows.anchor: Korah, a wealthy member of Pharaoh’s court, says in 28:78

words: فَمَآ أَغْنَىٰ عَنْهُم مَّا كَانُوا۟ يَكْسِبُونَ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: What those earlier people earned did not help them in this life or the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: in this life and the Hereafter that which they used to earn availed them not (cf. 15:84; 40:82)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The particle mā can be read negatively, yielding the translation that their earnings did not avail them.
rows.anchor: here rendered as a negative particle

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: If mā is interrogative rather than negative, the phrase asks how their earnings could have helped them.
rows.anchor: it would then read, “Then in what way did that which they used to earn avail them?” (Q)

words: فَمَآ أَغْنَىٰ عَنْهُم مَّا كَانُوا۟ يَكْسِبُونَ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Both readings stress the fragility and ephemerality of worldly pursuits before God reveals what people did not reckon with and wealth and children fail to help, except for a sound heart.
rows.anchor: Both renderings indicate the frailty and ephemerality of the things that consume people in this life

words: وَسِيقَ ٱلَّذِينَ كَفَرُوٓا۟ إِلَىٰ جَهَنَّمَ زُمَرًا
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those with heavy scales are separated from those with light scales; the latter are thrust into Hell violently.
rows.anchor: Those whose scales are heavy with good deeds will then be separated from those whose scales are light

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening of Hell’s gates is compared with 16:29.
rows.anchor: After the gates of Hell are opened (cf. 16:29)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hell’s keepers are said to be nineteen angels.
rows.anchor: its keepers, who are said to be nineteen angels (see 74:30c)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The keepers’ question about messengers is rhetorical rebuke, with parallels in 40:50 and 67:8–9.
rows.anchor: ask the disbelievers this rhetorical question by way of rebuke (cf. 40:50; 67:8–9)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The disbelievers admit a warner came, but say they denied him and claimed God sent nothing down; they recognize that listening and understanding would have kept them from the Blaze.
rows.anchor: The disbelievers will answer in the affirmative, saying, Indeed, a warner came unto us, but we denied him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their late admission cannot avert punishment because they were warned and given ample opportunity to repent; thus the Word of punishment came due.
rows.anchor: their now belated affirmation can do nothing to forestall their impending punishment

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After admitting their error, the disbelievers are cast into Hell.
rows.anchor: the disbelievers are then cast into Hell
